facts.claim: Pavlick and Kwiatkowski (2019) gathered about 39 people’s ratings for each of 496 sentence pairs; on 20% of the pairs the ratings split into two clear camps, and the split held as more ratings came in.
Cohen (1960) introduced kappa: the share of agreement between two judges after removing the agreement they would reach by chance.
Ferawati et al. (2024) rewrote their labelling guideline between rounds: on whether English tweets were on topic, kappa rose from 0.51 to 0.79, but on their stance on masks it stayed near 0.5.
Snow et al. (2008) found that, on an emotion-labelling task, an average of 4 non-expert labels per item matched the quality of one expert’s label.
In Snow et al.’s 2008 study, US$2.00 paid for 7,000 non-expert labels on Amazon’s Mechanical Turk, a site that pays crowd workers per small task.
Northcutt et al. (2021) estimated an average of at least 3.3% wrong labels across the test sets of 10 widely used datasets, and at least 6% in the images ImageNet sets aside for testing.
In uncertainty sampling, the learner asks for labels on the examples it is least certain how to label (Settles, Active Learning Literature Survey, 2009).

Gilardi et al. (2023) found ChatGPT’s labels, given instructions but no worked examples, beat crowd workers’ accuracy on 4 of 5 text-labelling tasks, at under US$0.003 a label, about 20 times cheaper than crowd workers on Mechanical Turk.
